addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude.ai Dropbox
# Claude App MCP LLM Boot Instructions

You are the assistant for Dropbox's Claude App MCP server. Your goal is to help users complete Dropbox tasks quickly and correctly while minimizing friction.

## Customer Use Cases

This app is best at helping users do these Dropbox workflows:

- Browse folder contents and paginate through large directories.
- Find files quickly using plain-language search terms and then open files with follow-on tools.
- Inspect file metadata (size, type, timestamps, IDs, sharing context).
- Check signed-in Dropbox identity, team/account context, and namespace-root context.
- Read text content from supported files up to 5 MiB, and provide a usable Dropbox link even when text extraction fails.
- Generate single-use temporary download links when the user explicitly needs direct file download URLs.
- Generate file previews with thumbnail and "open in Dropbox" experiences.
- Create folders in the right destination before saving artifacts.
- Create new text files directly in Dropbox.
- Create share links for files/folders and return the effective sharing settings.
- Inspect and list existing shared links.
- List, inspect, and create Dropbox file requests.
- Move, rename, copy, and delete Dropbox files/folders after explicit confirmation.
- Check the status of long-running move, copy, and delete jobs.

When users ask "what can you do?", summarize these use cases in plain language before taking action.

## Not Supported (Do Not Advertise)

- Editing or overwriting existing file content in place.
- Saving URL-hosted files directly into Dropbox.
- Uploading local/binary artifacts via `upload_file`.
- Permanent file deletion or wipe workflows. `delete` moves items to the user's Dropbox "Deleted files" area only.
- Reliable text extraction for supported files via `fetch`; extraction may still fail for some files, in which case the tool error may include a usable link.
- E-signature initiation or signing workflows.
- Actions outside Dropbox content management and sharing.

## Core Behavior

- Prioriti… [truncated]

## devonthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. (2) Output protection: result lists from tools like search_records, classify_record, find_similar_records, get_record_children, get_record_duplicates, and the link traversal tools are filt… [truncated]

## omnifocus
OmniFocus is a GTD task manager. Hierarchy: Folders > Projects > Tasks > Subtasks.

TASK STATES: Available, Blocked, Deferred (future defer date), Flagged, Overdue, Completed, Dropped. Planned Date is a scheduling signal only — no availability/overdue constraints.

PROJECT TYPES: "sequential" (tasks in order; first incomplete = available, rest blocked; position = dependencies), "parallel" (all available), "single_actions" (no completion goal, cannot auto-complete). The `next` field is true for the first available action in a sequential project/action group; in parallel projects, all incomplete tasks have `next: true`.

ACTION GROUPS: Task with subtasks. Parent shows `blocked: true` while subtasks are active — this is normal, not an error. Do not try to unblock it.

INHERITED STATUS: `completed`/`dropped` reflect the task's own state, not its container's. `effectivelyCompleted`/`effectivelyDropped` reflect the container's state — if true, the task's parent project or action group was completed/dropped. Task in completed project: `completed: false`, `effectivelyCompleted: true`, `available: false`. Use `available_only=True` for actionable tasks.

EFFECTIVE DATES: Dates returned by get_tasks are always effective (inherited). A task with no direct due date WILL show its project's due date in the dueDate field — this is correct behavior, not a bug. You cannot clear an inherited date at the task level. Write operations set the task's own date.

RECURRING TASKS: `completed=True` uses `mark complete`, which creates the next occurrence. This is guaranteed. WARNING: Dropping a recurring task (status='dropped') without clearing recurrence first (recurrence='') spawns the next occurrence. To stop a series: update_tasks([{"id": "...", "recurrence": "", "status": "dropped"}]).

TAGS: Represent work contexts. Tag statuses: Active (normal), On Hold (tasks excluded from Available perspective), Dropped (tag hidden from picker; does NOT affect task availability).

DEFER vs DUE: Defer = hidden until that date. Due = deadline.

- codebase-design: Shared vocabulary for designing deep modules. Use when the user wants to design or improve a module's interface, find deepening opportunities, decide where a seam goes, make code more testable or AI-navigable, or when another skill needs the deep-module vocabulary.
- diagnosing-bugs: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.
- domain-modeling: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when the user wants to pin down domain terminology or a ubiquitous language, record an architectural decision, or when another skill needs to maintain the domain model.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- grilling: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan or design. Use when the user wants to stress-test a plan before building, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.
- prototype: Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question. Use when the user wants to sanity-check whether a state model or logic feels right, or explore what a UI should look like.
- research: Investigate a question against high-trust primary sources and capture the findings as a Markdown file in the repo. Use when the user wants a topic researched, docs or API facts gathered, or reading legwork delegated to a background agent.
- seo-optimizer: Optimize content for search engines with keyword analysis, readability scoring, meta descriptions, and competitor comparison. Use this when users want to improve SEO, optimize blog posts, or analyze content for search performance.
- systems-thinking: Analyze problems using a Systems Thinking approach. Use when users mention "systems thinking," "systemic," "feedback loops," "unintended consequences," "root cause," "interconnected," or request analysis of complex, multi-factor problems. Guides conversation through questions and observations rather than prescriptive solutions.
- tdd: Test-driven development. Use when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions "red-green-refactor", or wants integration tests.
- add-backlinks: Add backlinks from related blog posts and glossary entries to a target post. Use when the user wants to improve internal linking by having other content link back to a specific article.
- blog-post: Create or revise a blog post for the Agile Pain Relief website. Use when the user wants to write a new blog post, revise/refresh an existing one, or update content. Guides through gathering information, content structure, internal linking, and post-publish steps.
- evergreen-posting: Compile Mark's selected social drafts into the batch JSON the posting pipeline consumes (LinkedIn / Mastodon / Bluesky), validating character limits and URL budgets, threading the link when it won't fit, and marking the source calendars so nothing is promoted twice. Blog/glossary/newsletter prose is authored and selected UPSTREAM as Markdown via the vault linkedin-style draft skill; this skill condenses the selected options to three platforms and writes the JSON, it does not re-draft that prose. Quiz posts are still drafted here from seeds. Use when Mark says "build the batch JSON", "compile the selected drafts", "schedule social media", or asks for the evergreen batch.
- glossary-entry: Create a new glossary term for the Agile Pain Relief website. Use when the user wants to add a new Agile/Scrum term definition, concept explanation, or methodology entry to the glossary.
- indexing-strategy: Use this skill when Mark asks to analyze, plan, or implement SEO topic clusters and internal linking for agilepainrelief.com. Covers two modes: (1) ANALYZE mode — audit existing content, identify pillar/cluster opportunities, find gaps and orphaned pages, and produce a prioritized action plan; (2) IMPLEMENT mode — generate specific internal linking instructions, write or revise blog posts and glossary entries to fit the cluster strategy, and produce per-page checklists. Also use when Mark asks what a blog post or glossary entry needs for SEO, or when he wants to check whether a draft meets the cluster linking requirements.
- newsletter: Draft and send a newsletter to the Newsletter Subscribers list via Cakemail, starting from plain markdown. Use when Mark wants to write, render, test, or dispatch a newsletter / email campaign, or turn a markdown file into a Cakemail draft campaign. Drives the email-automation CLI's send-newsletter command.
- social-media-adapt: Adapt LinkedIn posts to Mastodon and Bluesky formats with platform-specific character limits, thread formatting, and JSON structure. Use when Claude needs to convert LinkedIn content to other social platforms, create threaded posts, or adapt content for different character limits (Mastodon 500 chars, Bluesky 290 chars).
- claude-md-management:revise-claude-md: Update CLAUDE.md with learnings from this session
- claude-md-management:claude-md-improver: Audit and improve CLAUDE.md files in repositories. Use when user asks to check, audit, update, improve, or fix CLAUDE.md files. Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

---
title: 'Where is the Scrum Master role going in an AI world?'
description: 'Eight quick questions about how you actually spent the last couple of sprints. See which parts of your role are getting more valuable, and which parts the tools are starting to do.'
resultStyle: 'map-move'
# The email is asked for after the last question, before the map. The cover says
# so up front (heroButtonNote + intro), so nobody is ambushed by the ask; the
# trade is volume at the top of the funnel for people who finish the questions.
capturePosition: 'end'
# Shuffle each question's answers so the slipping/mixed/gaining/context order
# never telegraphs the "best" pick.
randomizeOptions: 'shuffle'

heroHeading: 'Where is the Scrum Master role going in an AI world?'
heroBody: 'Eight quick questions about how you actually spent the last couple of sprints. See which parts of your role are getting more valuable, and which parts the tools are starting to do.'
heroButtonLabel: 'Start the quiz'
# States the email ask on the cover, right under the button that starts the quiz.
heroButtonNote: 'Free, and about three minutes. You’ll add your email address after the last question, before I show you your map.'
# Labels the button that finishes the quiz, which here is the capture form's.
submitButtonLabel: 'Show me my map'

# The cover's three-step strip: what the taker gets, shown before the opt-in.
howItWorks:
  - label: 'step 1'
    title: 'Answer 8 questions'
    body: 'Think back over your last couple of sprints and answer honestly.'
    icon: 'steps'
    tone: 'accent'
  - label: 'step 2'
    title: 'See your map'
    body: 'A clear picture of the work that’s getting more valuable, and the work the tools are starting to do.'
    icon: 'map'
    tone: 'valuable'
  - label: 'step 3'
    title: 'Get one thing to try'
    body: 'The single change I’d make first, plus what else is worth a look.'
    icon: 'next'
    tone: 'alt'

introHeading: 'Before you start'
introIcon: 'privacy'

intro: |
  This isn’t a test. There’s no right answer, no score, and nobody else sees what you pick, not your manager, not your team. Take a moment and think about the last couple of sprints your team had, and when you answer, take the time to think about what actually happened.

  The quiz is here to help you think about the role and find a way to improve. After the last question I’ll ask for your email address, and then you get your map.

categoriesHeading: 'The three parts of the role this maps'

persuasion: |
  This isn’t a personality quiz. I hate those too. I won’t sugarcoat the challenges, but I do recognize that you work in the real world.

persuasionBullets:
  - 'Free'
  - 'Eight quick questions, about three minutes'
  - 'Immediate results, no waiting'
  - 'The work getting more valuable, and the work the tools are starting to do'
  - 'Clear, honest recommendations you can act on'
  - 'No archetype, no score for the wall, no gobbledygook'

captureHeading: 'Where should I send your result?'
captureBody: 'That was the last question. Add your email address and I’ll show you your map.'
# No captureButtonLabel: this button finishes the quiz, so it falls back to
# submitButtonLabel ("Show me my map"), which is exactly what it does.
captureFootnote: 'You’ll also join my email list for Scrum Masters navigating GenAI. No spam. Unsubscribe anytime.'

# Segments quiz takers so a future nurture sequence can trigger on this tag.
# Cakemail lowercases tags and auto-creates them on first submission.
submissionTags: ['sm-role-ai']

sections:
  - id: time
    label: 'Where your time goes'
    blurb: 'How you actually spent the hours over the last couple of sprints.'
  - id: coaching
    label: 'Growing the team'
    blurb: 'Coaching people, the Product Owner, and the team’s craft.'
  - id: system
    label: 'The system around the team'
    blurb: 'Impediments and the wider system beyond your own team.'

questions:
  - id: q1
    section: time
    text: 'Think back over the last couple of sprints. When you look at where the hours really went, what took up most of them?'
    options:
      - text: 'Running the Scrum events and keeping the team coordinated. That was most of it.'
        score: 0
        bucket: slipping
        icon: 'time'
        mapSentence: 'A lot of your time went to running the Scrum events and keeping the team coordinated. That’s busywork and it’s the least of what makes you valuable.'
        reclaimSentence: 'Reclaim the time. Running the events and keeping everyone coordinated is the first place to lean on a tool or trim back. It’s expensive because it takes time away from the real value of facilitation and coaching.'
      - text: 'A fairly even split between keeping things running and the harder human work.'
        score: 1
        bucket: mixed
      - text: 'Mostly the human stuff: conversations, working through conflict, helping people get aligned.'
        score: 2
        bucket: gaining
        icon: 'people'
        mapSentence: 'Most of your time went to the hard human work: conversations, conflict, getting people aligned. That’s the part of the role GenAI can’t replace, because it comes from building trust.'
      - text: 'Scrum events plus doing my own delivery work (coding, testing, and the like).'
        score: 0
        bucket: context
        icon: 'handsOn'
        mapSentence: 'Your hours are split between the role and delivery work, so there’s simply less Scrum Master time to spend. Judge it by what you did with the hours you had, not the ones you didn’t.'

  - id: q2
    section: time
    text: 'Picture the last few people who came to you for something. What did they actually want?'
    options:
      - text: 'Status, scheduling, a process question, or how to do something in our tool.'
        score: 0
        bucket: slipping
        icon: 'admin'
        mapSentence: 'People come to you for status and logistics. Useful, but it’s the errand the tools will absorb.'
        reclaimSentence: 'Reclaim the time. Being the status-and-logistics desk is the first thing to hand off or automate. Take that time and put it towards coaching and facilitation.'
      - text: 'Help getting a blocker out of the way.'
        score: 1
        bucket: mixed
      - text: 'Judgment, coaching, or help getting past something knotty and human.'
        score: 2

Read the live quiz frontmatter first — the headline you're revising sits in two places, `title` and `heroHeading` (`src/content/quizzes/scrum-master-ai/index.mdx:2,13`), currently both *"Where is the Scrum Master role going in an AI world?"*

## Feedback on your draft

> GenAI is changing the we work. How is the ScrumMaster role changing?

**Typo:** "the we work" → "the way we work".

**The first sentence is doing no work.** "GenAI is changing the way we work" is a premise nobody in your audience disputes and everybody has read 400 times this year. It spends half the headline establishing something the reader already granted before they arrived. Cut it and you lose nothing.

**The second sentence is third person, which is the opposite of personalizing.** "How is the ScrumMaster role changing?" is an industry question: the kind of thing a conference talk answers. Your quiz doesn't answer it. Your quiz answers *"which parts of **your** last two sprints are gaining value and which are slipping"*. The headline should promise the personal readout, because that's the thing the reader can only get by taking it. An abstract question invites them to think "good question, I'll read someone's blog post about it".

**It excludes three quarters of your stated audience.** Part-time SM, PM, and Manager don't have "ScrumMaster" on their badge. Your current live headline has the same problem. Either name the work rather than the title, or name the group explicitly.

**Consistency:** the rest of the quiz says "Scrum Master" (two words). Don't mix in "ScrumMaster" here.

**Length:** `heroHeading` renders serif in a ~680px column, so much past ~65 characters wraps to three lines. Your draft is 76 and reads as two headlines stacked.

---

## 10 alternatives

**Personal inventory** (matches what the quiz actually delivers)

1. Which parts of your Scrum Master week is AI about to do for you?
2. Where did your last two sprints go, and which of it survives AI?
3. Map your Scrum Master week: what's gaining value, what the tools are taking.
4. Your role, sorted: the work AI can't touch and the work it already does.
5. How much of your last sprint could a tool have done?

**Direct challenge** (shorter, punchier, more scroll-stopping)

6. GenAI can already do parts of your job. Which parts?
7. AI is taking parts of the Scrum Master role. Find out which are yours.
8. You do the Scrum Master work. Which of it still needs a human?

**Title-neutral** (opens the door to the PM, manager, and part-time SM)

9. If you look after how the team works, which of it still needs you?
10. GenAI is absorbing the coordination work. What's left is your real job.

---

**My pick: #1.** It's second person, it's specific to a week rather than a career, "about to" gives it urgency without the failure framing you deliberately kept out of the results page, and at 64 characters it holds two lines. #6 is the strongest if you want something blunter, and it's the only one under 55 characters.

Two knock-on edits if you take a title-neutral option (#9, #10): the `captureFootnote` still says "for Scrum Masters navigating GenAI", and the `categoriesHeading` says "the three parts of the role" — both would need widening to match, or the promise breaks between headline and form.

content.text:
## On your line

Grammar's fine (`AI` is the subject of `is`). But the swap of `your` → `the` trades away the personalization and buys almost no inclusivity, because the word excluding your manager isn't `your`, it's `Scrum Master`. A manager reading "the Scrum Master role" still sees a headline about somebody else's job; the Scrum Master reading it now sees an essay question instead of a mirror. It loses on both ends of the trade.

## The bigger constraint

I read all eight question stems (`index.mdx:84-254`). Every one is first-person and about work you personally did: "where the hours really went", "came to **you**", "**your** time", "when did **you** last sit with someone", "what did **you** actually do", "**your** Product Owner".

That splits your audience list in two, and the split isn't the one you'd expect:

- **Fully served today:** Scrum Master, part-time SM, and Project Manager. A PM who runs the standups, chases status, and updates Jira answers all eight questions honestly, and gets a genuinely useful map. The only thing keeping them out is the *label* on the door.
- **Not served by a single question:** a manager who has Scrum Masters rather than being one. They'd hit q1 and have to answer about someone else's hours. A headline can get them to click; q1 loses them.

So the headline is the right fix for three of your four personas, and the wrong tool for the fourth. Widening the wording won't reach the manager-of-SMs. Reaching them needs either a "answer for the Scrum Master on your team" instruction in the intro, or a separate quiz.

## Headlines that actually widen

Name the *work* instead of the title, and keep the second person:

1. **Which parts of keeping your team running is AI about to do for you?** (67 chars) — the PM and the part-time SM both do this; nobody needs a badge to qualify.
2. **Which parts of the Scrum Master job still need a person?** (56) — genuinely dual-readable: the SM hears "what makes me valuable", the manager hears "what am I staffing for". The only one of these that a manager can read as being about their decision.
3. **You keep the team running. Which parts of that is AI about to do?** (65) — the short first clause does the qualifying, so no title is needed at all.

My pick is **#1** if you want the SM/PM/part-timer, **#2** if the manager genuinely matters.

## Do the inviting in the subhead, not the headline

The headline can carry a sharp personal pull or a wide door, not both. `heroBody` is two free lines sitting directly underneath it. Something like:

```yaml
heroBody: 'Eight quick questions about how you actually spent the last couple of sprints. See which parts of the work are getting more valuable, and which parts the tools are starting to do. Works whether you hold the title, cover it alongside delivery work, or run the process as a PM.'
```

That last sentence does more inclusion work than any headline wording will, and it costs the headline nothing.

Two knock-ons if you go this way: `captureFootnote` still says "for Scrum Masters navigating GenAI" and `categoriesHeading` says "the three parts of the role" (`index.mdx:48,64`). Both would need the same widening or the promise breaks between the hero and the form.
Let's go with 2 and tweak the subhead

content.text:
Three surfaces, three jobs. `bodyText` is shared by the banner and the modal; `subHeading` is banner-only; the sidebar has its own defaults hardcoded in the component. Here's what I'd change, and why each one differs.

### `src/constants/cta.ts`

```ts
heading: 'Which parts of the Scrum Master job still need a person?',
subHeading: 'Eight questions, about three minutes. No score, no archetype.',
modalHeading: 'Which parts of your job still need a person?',
modalButtonText: 'Show Me the Map',
bodyText:
  'Some of the Scrum Master job is getting more valuable, and some of it is quietly being absorbed by tools. Answer eight questions about how you actually spent your last couple of sprints, and you’ll get a map of which is which, plus the one change I’d make first.',
buttonText: 'Show Me the Map',
```

- **`heading`** takes the landing headline verbatim. The banner sits inline on the homepage and index pages where the reader is scanning, not being interrupted, so it can afford the full 56 characters and the exact message match is worth more than brevity.
- **`modalHeading` drops "Scrum Master"** and goes second person. The modal fires 30 seconds into a blog post, so it gets about two seconds of attention and needs to be shorter. It can drop the title because the surrounding page already establishes the context, and *"your job"* hits harder on an interrupt than a job title does. The shared phrase "still need a person" keeps the match with the landing page intact.
- **`bodyText`**: "role" → "job" to match the new headline, and the opening "Parts of…" → "Some of…" because "parts" is now in the heading directly above it and repeating it reads flabby. Otherwise unchanged.
- **`buttonText`**: "See Where Your Role Stands" was written against the old *where is this going* framing and no longer answers the new headline's question. Making it match `modalButtonText` also gives you one consistent phrase across banner, modal, and the quiz's own finishing button ("Show me my map"). If you'd rather keep them distinct, **"Map My Last Two Sprints"** is the alternative I'd pick: more concrete, tells them the work is small.

The doc comment at `cta.ts:45` quotes the old heading and describes the old hook, so it needs the same update.

### `src/components/global/link-sidebar.astro`

```astro
heading = 'Which parts of the Scrum Master job still need a person?',
body = 'Eight questions. Three minutes. See which parts of the work are getting more valuable, and which parts the tools are starting to do. No score, no archetype, just what I see and where I’d start.',
```

Full headline here: the sidebar sits beside the article, gets read at browsing pace, and isn't interrupting anything. Only change to `body` is "your role" → "the work", matching the landing page. I'd leave `linkText` as "Take the Quiz" — it's a passive-browsing surface, so plain and descriptive beats clever.

### What I'd leave alone

`subHeading` (banner h3) still reads well and does the reassurance job. The audience-widening sentence stays on the landing page only: on a banner it costs a line and dilutes the hook, and by the time someone reaches the landing page they get it anyway.

Want me to apply all of this?

## 2026-07-30 — Quiz headline rewritten, and the sidebar CTA moved into `cta.ts`

**Why.** "Where is the Scrum Master role going in an AI world?" was a third-person
industry question. The quiz doesn't answer that; it answers "which parts of _your_
last two sprints are gaining value and which are slipping". A headline that poses
an essay question invites the reader to go find someone's blog post about it. The
new one, "Which parts of the Scrum Master job still need a person?", promises the
personal readout the quiz actually delivers, and reads two ways on purpose: the
Scrum Master hears "what makes me valuable", a manager hears "what am I staffing
for".

**The audience question we did not fully solve.** Mark wanted a manager who isn't
a Scrum Master to see themselves here. All eight questions are first-person and
about work you personally did ("came to _you_", "_your_ time", "what did _you_
actually do"), so the split isn't by job title. A Project Manager or part-time
Scrum Master who runs the events and chases status answers all eight honestly and
gets a useful map; only the label was keeping them out, which the widened
`heroBody` fixes. A manager _of_ Scrum Masters is served by no question in the
quiz, and no headline wording changes that. Reaching them needs either an
"answer for the Scrum Master on your team" instruction in the intro (the map
sentences are second person, so it would read slightly off), or a separate quiz.
Left undone deliberately rather than papered over with an invitation q1 breaks.

**Three surfaces, three registers.** The banner and the blog/glossary sidebar
carry the landing page's headline verbatim, because both are read at browsing
pace and exact message match beats brevity. The modal fires 30 seconds into a
post and gets about two seconds of attention, so it drops the job title and goes
second person. The shared phrase "still need a person" is what keeps all three
matched to the landing page.

**`link-sidebar.astro` no longer owns copy.** It had its own hardcoded heading,
body, link text, image and alt as prop defaults, which is how it came to be
advertising the old headline after the quiz had moved on. Both callers render
`<LinkSidebar />` bare, so the props were dead flexibility hiding a drift hazard.
Copy now comes from `CTA_PRIMARY` (new `sidebarBody` / `sidebarButtonText`
fields) and imagery from a new `SIDEBAR_IMAGES`, matching how `cta-banner.astro`
and `modal-popup.astro` already read the constants. `src/constants/cta.ts` is now
the only file to edit for CTA copy on all three surfaces.

355	- Adding redirects from a page's own path to itself with a trailing slash (e.g., `'/glossary': '/glossary/'`). Netlify already handles trailing slash normalization, so this creates an infinite redirect loop
356	
357	## CTA / Popup System
358	
359	Centralized in `src/constants/cta.ts` with two rendering components:
360	
361	- `src/components/global/modal-popup.astro` — Popup on blog and glossary pages (30s delay, 15-day frequency cap)
362	- `src/components/global/cta-banner.astro` — Inline banner on homepage, blog index, and glossary index
363	
364	**How it works:**
365	
366	- `CTA_PRIMARY: CTAContent` — The active CTA copy (heading, body, button text, link)
367	- `CTA_VARIANT: CTAContent | null` — Set to `null` when no A/B test is running; populate with a `CTAContent` object to activate a second variant
368	- `AB_TEST_ENABLED` — Master switch; when `false`, always shows primary
369	- Both components conditionally render the variant block only when `CTA_VARIANT` is not null
370	- PostHog tracks button clicks via `data-ph-capture-attribute-*` attributes
371	- Modal frequency controlled via localStorage (`src/utils/storage.ts`)
372	
373	**To update CTA copy:** Edit `CTA_PRIMARY` in `src/constants/cta.ts`. No component changes needed.
374	**CTA forms vs link buttons:** All popup/banner CTAs render a link button. - Adding redirects from a page's own path to itself with a trailing slash (e.g., `'/glossary': '/glossary/'`). Netlify already handles trailing slash normalization, so this creates an infinite redirect loop

## CTA / Popup System

Centralized in `src/constants/cta.ts` with two rendering components:

- `src/components/global/modal-popup.astro` — Popup on blog and glossary pages (30s delay, 15-day frequency cap)
- `src/components/global/cta-banner.astro` — Inline banner on homepage, blog index, and glossary index

**How it works:**

- `CTA_PRIMARY: CTAContent` — The active CTA copy (heading, body, button text, link)
- `CTA_VARIANT: CTAContent | null` — Set to `null` when no A/B test is running; populate with a `CTAContent` object to activate a second variant
- `AB_TEST_ENABLED` — Master switch; when `false`, always shows primary
- Both components conditionally render the variant block only when `CTA_VARIANT` is not null
- PostHog tracks button clicks via `data-ph-capture-attribute-*` attributes
- Modal frequency controlled via localStorage (`src/utils/storage.ts`)

**To update CTA copy:** Edit `CTA_PRIMARY` in `src/constants/cta.ts`. No component changes needed.
**CTA forms vs link buttons:** All popup/banner CTAs render a link button. The shared `FormSubmission` component (used by the newsletter section of pages, the modal popup, and the CTA banner) POSTs (Turnstile-gated) to `/api/newsletter-signup`, which forwards to Cakemail's Newsletter Subscribers form server-side. Its `source` prop applies a per-placement signup tag; see "General newsletter signup" above.
**To run an A/B test:** Populate `CTA_VARIANT` with a `CTAContent` object and set `AB_TEST_ENABLED = true`.

content.text:
All applied and verified: `npx astro check` reports 0 errors / 0 warnings / 0 hints, `npm run lint:tw` is clean, and the production build succeeds with the new heading present in the rendered pages.

**`src/constants/cta.ts`** — the copy changes as proposed (`heading`, `modalHeading`, `bodyText`, `buttonText`), plus two new required `CTAContent` fields, `sidebarBody` and `sidebarButtonText`, and a new `SIDEBAR_IMAGES` export carrying the image and its alt text. I rewrote the `CTA_PRIMARY` doc comment: it quoted the old heading, and it now records the three-surfaces-three-registers reasoning so the next person doesn't "fix" the modal's shorter heading into consistency and break the interrupt.

**`src/components/global/link-sidebar.astro`** — copy props removed entirely rather than re-pointed at the constants. Both callers render `<LinkSidebar />` bare, so the props were unused flexibility, and they're precisely how the component ended up advertising a headline the quiz had moved on from. It now reads `CTA_PRIMARY` and `SIDEBAR_IMAGES` directly, matching how `cta-banner.astro` and `modal-popup.astro` already work. Net 33 lines down to 21.

**Two notes on the image.** The sidebar and modal use the same asset, so I imported it a second time under `SidebarImage` rather than reusing `ModalImage` — the two surfaces can now diverge without one silently changing the other, and Vite dedupes the asset so there's no weight cost. Separately, the existing comment in `cta.ts` is right that both images are leftovers from the AI-failure-modes campaign and are about GenAI coding, not the Scrum Master role; that mismatch is now three surfaces wide.

Also updated `HISTORY.md` (new dated entry, including the manager-persona gap we left open deliberately) and the CTA section of `CLAUDE.md`, which said "two rendering components" and no longer knew about the sidebar.

`.claude/settings.local.json` also shows in the diff — that's a permission entry the harness added while running the build, not something I edited.

1	# Project History
2	
3	A short, human-readable log of notable changes and the reasoning behind them.
4	Newest first. (Detailed, current behaviour lives in `CLAUDE.md`; this file is the
5	"why we did it" story.)
6	
7	## 2026-07-30 — Quiz headline rewritten, and the sidebar CTA moved into `cta.ts`
8	
9	**Why.** "Where is the Scrum Master role going in an AI world?" was a third-person
10	industry question. The quiz doesn't answer that; it answers "which parts of _your_
11	last two sprints are gaining value and which are slipping". A headline that poses
12	an essay question invites the reader to go find someone's blog post about it. The
13	new one, "Which parts of the Scrum Master job still need a person?", promises the
14	personal readout the quiz actually delivers, and reads two ways on purpose: the
15	Scrum Master hears "what makes me valuable", a manager hears "what am I staffing
16	for".
17	
18	**The audience question we did not fully solve.** Mark wanted a manager who isn't
19	a Scrum Master to see themselves here. All eight questions are first-person and
20	about work you personally did ("came to _you_", "_your_ time", "what did _you_
21	actually do"), so the split isn't by job title. A Project Manager or part-time
22	Scrum Master who runs the events and chases status answers all eight honestly and
23	gets a useful map; only the label was keeping them out, which the widened
24	`heroBody` fixes. A manager _of_ Scrum Masters is served by no question in the
25	quiz, and no headline wording changes that. Reaching them needs either an
26	"answer for the Scrum Master on your team" instruction in the intro (the map
27	sentences are second person, so it would read slightly off), or a separate quiz.
28	Left undone deliberately rather than papered over with an invitation q1 breaks.
29	
30	**Three surfaces, three registers.** The banner and the blog/glossary sidebar
31	carry the landing page's headline verbatim, because both are read at browsing
32	pace and exact message match beats brevity. The modal fires 30 seconds into a
33	post and gets about two seconds of attention, so it drops the job title and goes
34	second person. The shared phrase "still need a person" is what keeps all three
35	matched to the landing page.
36	
37	**`link-sidebar.astro` no longer owns copy.** It had its own hardcoded heading,
38	body, link text, image and alt as prop defaults, which is how it came to be
39	advertising the old headline after the quiz had moved on. Both callers render
40	`<LinkSidebar />` bare, so the props were dead flexibility hiding a drift hazard.
41	Copy now comes from `CTA_PRIMARY` (new `sidebarBody` / `sidebarButtonText`
42	fields) and imagery from a new `SIDEBAR_IMAGES`, matching how `cta-banner.astro`
43	and `modal-popup.astro` already read the constants. `src/constants/cta.ts` is now
44	the only file to edit for CTA copy on all three surfaces.
45	
46	## 2026-07-30 — Quiz email capture moved back to the end, with the ask stated on the cover
47	
48	**Why.** The hard gate worked (signups arrive, Turnstile holds), but asking for
49	an email before question 1 charges the visitor before they've seen anything.
50	Someone who has answered eight questions has already invested; someone who has
51	read a cover has not. Moving the ask back to the end trades a self-qualified,
52	smaller list for a larger one, and the reflective `map-move` result is the kind
53	of thing people want _after_ the thinking, not a prize they bid on up front.
54	
55	**What we did.** `scrum-master-ai` frontmatter went back to
56	`capturePosition: 'end'`. The engine already supported both positions, so no
57	engine code changed: the stepper puts the "Before you start" card back as step 0
58	under the cover, the hero's own "Start the quiz" button returns, and the capture
59	card (first name optional + email) becomes the last step. `captureButtonLabel`
60	was dropped so the capture button falls back to `submitButtonLabel`, "Show me my
61	map", which is now literally what it does; `captureBody` was added because the
62	end capture renders a paragraph the compact gate had no room for.
63	
64	**The cover still says the email is coming.** That was the one thing worth
65	keeping from the gate: nobody should meet the form as a surprise. `heroButtonNote`
66	under the start button and the closing line of `intro` both say the email is
67	asked for after the last question, before the map. The `heroButtonNote` field
68	exists for exactly this (it was added so the hero could never promise "at the
69	end" on a start-gated quiz) and it now earns its keep in the other direction.
70	
71	**Then the cover had to be rebalanced.** Restoring the end capture put the
72	"Before you start" card back into the stepper with its own button, so it went
73	from a short static block wedged mid-page to a tall centred island terminating
74	an otherwise left-aligned page. `QuizIntroCard` is now left-aligned like every
75	other block. The centring had been deliberate, and the component's comment
76	explained the reasoning correctly (centred lines get hard to track past ~46
77	characters), but it constrained the _measure_ and not the _length_: once the
78	copy grew to two paragraphs plus a button, centring stopped reading as a pause
79	and started reading as a different design language.
80	
81	**The email note was set as small print, which was backwards.** A quiz that
82	sells itself on candour cannot whisper the one thing it asks for. It moved from
83	muted `text-sm` to `text-base` italic in `ink-secondary`, held to the hero
84	body's measure so it reads as part of the pitch rather than a disclaimer under
85	the button.
86	
87	**One measure down the whole cover.** The hero paragraphs were capped at 52ch
88	while `QuizIntroCard` ran to 60ch, so the reading column narrowed and then
89	widened again on the way down the page, which is the sort of thing you feel
90	before you see. Everything on the cover is 60ch now. The card's text is still
91	inset by the card's own padding, so the left edges don't align and shouldn't:
92	it's the same measure, not the same margin.
93	
94	## 2026-07-29 — Blog/glossary sidebar was still selling the retired quiz
95	
96	**Why.** `link-sidebar.astro` takes every string as a prop, but both call sites
97	(`blog/[id].astro`, `glossary/[id].astro`) render `<LinkSidebar />` with no props
98	at all, so the component's _defaults_ are the live copy. Those defaults still
99	read "Twelve questions. Three minutes. Real studies, real citations." and linked
100	to `/quiz/ai-failure-modes/`. The link itself still worked (a redirect sends it
101	to `/quiz/scrum-master-ai/`), which is exactly why nobody noticed: the promise
102	was wrong, not the destination. A reader clicked through expecting twelve
103	questions on how GenAI fails and landed on eight questions about their own role.
104	
105	**What we did.** Rewrote the defaults for the current quiz: new heading, eight
106	questions, "no score, no archetype" (which is the whole point of the `map-move`
107	result style), and a direct link to `/quiz/scrum-master-ai/` rather than leaning
108	on the redirect. Also fixed `imageAlt`, which named the old quiz instead of
109	describing the image; it now matches the alt text on the source blog post.
110	
111	**Voice, and the quiz hero along with it.** The promo copy reuses the quiz's own
112	result headings verbatim: "getting more valuable", "the tools are starting to do
113	this", "where I'd start". The first draft instead said "gaining value" /
114	"quietly slipping away", lifted from the quiz's own `description` / `heroBody` /
115	`howItWorks` block, which turned out not to be Mark's voice either. So the same
116	substitution went into the quiz frontmatter: the landing page had been opening in
117	one voice and delivering its result eight questions later in another.
118	
119	The lesson for sampling voice: the **result** copy (`mapMove.*`, the
120	`mapSentence` / `reclaimSentence` / `redirectSentence` lines, the answer options)
121	is where Mark actually wrote; the hero/description block reads as

content.text:
Read all eight questions against the five personas, plus the engine's types and the map-move renderer. Two answers here: which questions break, and a mechanical problem that lands before any of them.

## The engine can't branch, so the classifier changes nothing downstream

`QuizQuestion` is `{ id, section, text, reveal, options }` (`src/lib/quiz-engine/types.ts:24`). There is no `showIf`, no per-role option set, no conditional skip. Everyone sees every question. So a role question cannot change what q1 to q8 ask, cannot reorder them, and cannot swap wording per persona. It's inert.

It's also not free:

- **Every option must carry a `score`**, so the classifier feeds `total`. Harmless under `map-move` (no number is printed) but it would corrupt any future `band` quiz that copies the pattern.
- **It lands in the balance bar** unless every option is `bucket: context`.
- **If you bucket it `context` with no `mapSentence`, the results page renders an empty row.** `MapMoveResults.astro:226-236` maps over `result.context` with no guard on a missing sentence: you'd get an icon and a blank line in the context strip. So each role option needs either its own `mapSentence` (which turns "I'm a project manager" into a result observation) or a one-line engine fix.
- **The role can't reach Cakemail.** `submissionTags` is a flat static list; there's no per-answer tag. So it can't segment the list either.

Net: today, a 9th question costs you a question's worth of drop-off at the point of highest abandonment and buys nothing that reaches the map or the list.

## Which questions break

| | SM | PT SM | PM | Team Member | Manager |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **q1** hours | ✓ | ✓ | ~ | **✗** | **✗** |
| **q2** what people want | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ~ | ✓ |
| **q3** Jira / status / reports | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ~ | ✓ |
| **q4** coaching people | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ~ | ✓ |
| **q5** team vs wider system | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **q6** last blocker | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| **q7** coaching the PO | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | **✗✗** | ✓ |
| **q8** team's craft | ✓ | ✓ | ~ | **✗** | ~ |

**Big rework: q1, q7, q8.** Everything else is a copy touch-up or fine as-is.

**q1** is the worst, because it's first and it's the only question where two personas have no honest answer. All four options presuppose you run Scrum events. A pure Team Member attends them; a Manager's hours go to 1:1s, hiring, escalation and stakeholders. Option 4 ("Scrum events plus doing my own delivery work") is the part-timer's answer and a Team Member will land on it wrongly. Even the Project Manager only half-fits: broadening "running the Scrum events" to "running the meetings and keeping the team coordinated" would carry them.

**q7 is the one that actively lies to a Team Member.** "Help your Product Owner improve at their own job" is not a Team Member's remit, so they pick option 1 ("that's not really something I do") and get told coaching the PO is the earliest and most important activity for a ScrumMaster and they're not doing it. A correct answer scored as a gap. Worse, q7 is second in `redirectPriority` (`index.mdx:278`), so it will frequently *win the move* and become the single recommendation they walk away with.

**q8 is inverted for a Team Member.** Option 1 is "that's on them or the tech lead, not my patch" — for a Team Member, craft *is* their patch, so the slipping option is unpickable and the only fitting answer is option 4, a `context` bucket that scores nothing.

**Small copy fixes: q2, q3, q4.** These travel, but q4's map sentence says "the highest-value thing a *Scrum Master* does" and q3's context option says "I'm only part-time *in this role*". A Manager or Team Member reading those gets someone else's label on their own result.

**q5 and q6 need nothing.** They're about attention and about what you did with a blocker, neither of which assumes a title. They're the model for what a persona-portable question looks like.

## The layer under the questions

There are roughly 30 `mapSentence` / `reclaimSentence` / `redirectSentence` strings and they are all written in Scrum Master voice ("the least of what makes *you* valuable", "one earliest and most important activities for a ScrumMaster"). Fixing the four questions does not fix the result. This is the larger half of the job and it's the half a role classifier makes *more* visible, because you'll have just told a Manager you know they're a Manager and then handed them a Scrum Master's map.

Correction to what I put in `HISTORY.md` yesterday: I wrote that a manager of Scrum Masters "is served by no question in the quiz." Having now read all eight against that persona, that's too strong. q4, q5 and q6 travel to a manager unchanged, and q2, q3, q7 travel with minor wording changes. It's q1 that breaks, plus the result copy. **Team Member**, not Manager, is the persona that genuinely breaks the quiz. Want me to fix that entry?

## What I'd actually do

## Capture position

The `capturePosition` frontmatter field decides where the email capture sits
(defaults to `'end'`):

- **`'end'`** — intro, then every question, then the capture form. Submitting
  delivers the contact and redirects to the results.
- **`'start'`** — the capture form as a **hard gate**, then the intro, then the
  questions. Submitting delivers the contact and advances; the last question's
  button is what finishes the quiz. The taker knows up front that an email is
  involved, and it self-qualifies for higher intent at the cost of some volume.
  The gate renders as a compact, **email-only** panel (no first-name field:
  every extra field on a gate costs completions), so it can sit inside the host
  page's cover layout rather than replacing it.

Whichever comes first is the step the host page's marketing chrome sits
alongside, so hide that chrome on `index !== 0` from `quiz:step-changed` rather
than keying on the step's `kind`.

Two consequences of a start gate worth knowing:

- **`levelTagPrefix` does nothing.** Nothing has been answered at submit time,
  so there is no result tier to tag with. Static `submissionTags` still apply.
- **The contact is delivered before the quiz is finished.** Someone who gates in
  and then abandons at question 3 is on your list without a result. That's the
  trade the position makes; if you need the result to reach the ESP, capture at
  the end.

Back-navigating onto an already-submitted gate does not re-deliver the contact;
the button just moves the taker forward.

## Look and feel

The engine ships one visual system rather than raw Tailwind defaults, because a
quiz reads as a single artefact. Two rules drive it:

## Profile questions

A question with `kind: 'profile'` classifies the **taker** instead of assessing
them. It is not part of the assessment, so it:

- contributes nothing to the score, the section scores, or the map;
- carries no progress bar and is excluded from the progress total, so a cover
  that promises "eight questions" stays true when you add one;
- always leads, in declared order, ahead of anything `randomize` does;
- keeps its declared option order even under `randomizeOptions: 'shuffle'`,
  because there is no "best" pick to hide and role lists have their own order.

Give it a `section` id that **isn't** one of your declared sections. No section
label then renders above it, and it adds no card to the landing page's section
list. `score` is still required on each option (the field is not optional); use
`0` and ignore it.

Its two payloads are per-option:

```yaml
- id: role
  section: profile
  kind: profile
  text: 'First, so I read your answers properly: which of these is closest to you?'
  options:
    - text: 'Scrum Master. It’s the job I’m hired to do.'
      score: 0
      tag: 'role-scrum-master'
    - text: 'Manager. I manage the Scrum Master, or the team, or both.'
      score: 0
      tag: 'role-manager'
      lens: 'Answering as a manager: think about where your Scrum Master spent their time, not where you spent yours.'
```

**`tag`** is applied to the submission when that answer is chosen, sent as
`tags[<name>]=true` alongside the host's static `submissionTags`. Tags from
multiple answers are deduped. Like `levelTagPrefix`, it needs answers to exist
at submit time, so **a start gate collects none of them** — profile tags only
reach the ESP with `capturePosition: 'end'`.

**`lens`** is a standing instruction for the rest of the quiz. It appears under
the options the moment that answer is picked, and again above every later
question. Reach for it when an answer changes *who the remaining questions are
about*: a manager taking a quiz whose every question says "you" will otherwise
answer about their own week and get a map of the wrong job. The repeat is the
point — a one-off note at question 0 is forgotten by question 3.

The profile answer does ride along in the `map-move` results query, so a results
page can branch on it later; the built-in renderer ignores it.

## 2026-07-30 — Quiz asks the taker's role first: `profile` questions, `tag`, `lens`

**Why.** The quiz reads as a Scrum Master's quiz, but the people taking it also
include part-time Scrum Masters, project managers running the process, and
managers of Scrum Masters. Knowing which one is in front of us is worth having
in Cakemail for segmentation, and for a manager it changes what the questions
even mean.

**Plain "Team Member" was deliberately dropped.** It was on the original list
and it was the one persona that genuinely broke the quiz: q7 (coaching the
Product Owner) and q8 (the team's craft) would have scored a team member's
_correct_ answers as gaps, and q7 sits second in `redirectPriority`, so that
misread would frequently have become the single recommendation they walked away
with. The role list is now Scrum Master / part-time Scrum Master / project
manager / manager, all of whom do the work the questions ask about.

**Three engine features, not a one-off.** The quiz engine is meant to be
extractable, so this went in as general capability:

- `kind: 'profile'` on a question. It classifies the taker rather than assessing
  them: no score, no map entry, no progress bar, and it always leads regardless
  of `randomize`. Excluding it from progress is what keeps the cover's promise of
  "eight questions" true without recounting, and excluding it from the map is
  what stops "I'm a project manager" appearing as a line in the context strip
  and skewing the balance bar.
- `tag` on an option, applied to the submission as `tags[<name>]=true` alongside
  the static `submissionTags`. This is what carries the role to Cakemail. Note it
  needs answers to exist at submit time, so like `levelTagPrefix` it collects
  nothing on a start gate.
- `lens` on an option: a standing instruction shown from the moment that answer
  is picked and repeated above every later question. Every question in this quiz
  says "you", so a manager would otherwise answer about their own week and get a
  map of the wrong job. The repeat is the point: a one-off note at question 0 is
  forgotten by question 3.

**Also fixed a latent bug next door.** `MapMoveResults.astro` rendered a context
answer with no `mapSentence` as a bare icon beside an empty line, and would have
rendered the panel as a heading over an empty list. Profile questions no longer
reach it, but the guard is right anyway.

**Still outstanding:** the eight questions and roughly thirty result sentences
are written in Scrum Master voice ("the highest-value thing a Scrum Master
does"). Now that the quiz knows it's talking to a manager or a project manager,
that mismatch is more visible, not less. The copy pass is the next job.

lines: **Submission flow.** Scoring runs in the browser (the engine is pure TypeScript). On capture submit the engine assembles `email`, `custom_attributes[firstname]`, and tags (`tags[<name>]=true` from `submissionTags`, plus an optional `levelTagPrefix` result-tier tag), then hands them to the Turnstile gate like the other forms: the APR wrapper `src/components/quiz/GatedQuizStepper.tsx` appends the token + `form=quiz` and POSTs to `/api/newsletter-signup` (see "Signup bot protection" above); on success the engine advances to question 1 (start gate) or redirects to `/quiz/{slug}/results/?...` with the locally-computed query string (end capture). **The engine itself stays APR-agnostic** via two generic hooks it exposes: `onSubmit(formData)` (host owns delivery; throwing keeps the user on the capture step to retry, resolving proceeds to results) and `captureExtras` (a `ReactNode` slot, used here to mount the Turnstile widget). The engine's built-in `cakemailFormUrl` no-cors path still exists for standalone use but is unused here — the frontmatter field and its `content.config.ts` schema entry were removed.

-**Audience and segmentation.** Quiz signups go to the general `Newsletter Subscribers` list (the same list as post-course and general signups). The current `scrum-master-ai` quiz tags submissions `sm-role-ai` (via `submissionTags`), so a future nurture sequence can trigger on that tag; Cakemail auto-creates the tag on first submission and lowercases it (see [[reference-cakemail-lowercase-tags]]). The quiz's capture copy tells users up front that they're subscribing to the list, so one list per consent is correct and the tag is the segmentation. The engine also supports a per-tier tag via the `levelTagPrefix` frontmatter field (for `map-move`, the tier is the framing bucket), but `scrum-master-ai` does not set it. The tag rides along in the same submission (`tags[sm-role-ai]=true`), forwarded by `/api/newsletter-signup` to the consolidated Cakemail form, so no dedicated quiz form is needed. (The retired `ai-failure-modes` quiz used the `aiquiz` tag; the two AI lead-magnet download forms still apply `aiquiz` — see "General newsletter signup" below.)

+**Profile questions.** A question with `kind: 'profile'` classifies the taker instead of assessing them: it is excluded from the score, from the map, and from the progress bar (so a cover promising "eight questions" stays honest), and it always leads regardless of `randomize`. Each of its options can carry a `tag` (applied to the submission as `tags[<name>]=true`, which is how the role reaches Cakemail) and a `lens` (a standing instruction shown from the moment that answer is picked and repeated above every later question). `scrum-master-ai` opens with one: Scrum Master / part-time Scrum Master / project manager / manager, tagged `role-*`. The manager option carries the `lens`, because every question after it says "you" and a manager would otherwise answer about their own week. Give a profile question a `section` id that is **not** one of the declared sections, or it adds a card to the landing page. Like `levelTagPrefix`, `tag` collects nothing on a start gate, since nothing is answered at submit time. Plain "team member" is deliberately not an option: q7 and q8 would score a team member's correct answers as gaps.

The engine also supports a per-tier tag via the `levelTagPrefix` frontmatter field (for `map-move`, the tier is the framing bucket), but `scrum-master-ai` does not set it. The tag rides along in the same submission (`tags[sm-role-ai]=true`), forwarded by `/api/newsletter-signup` to the consolidated Cakemail form, so no dedicated quiz form is needed. (The retired `ai-failure-modes` quiz used the `aiquiz` tag; the two AI lead-magnet download forms still apply `aiquiz` — see "General newsletter signup" below.)

content.text:
Done and verified in a real browser, not just by type-check.

## What went in

Three general engine features rather than a one-off, since the engine is meant to be extractable:

- **`kind: 'profile'`** on a question — classifies the taker instead of assessing them. No score, no map entry, **no progress bar**, and it always leads regardless of `randomize`. Excluding it from progress is what keeps "eight questions" true on the cover without recounting; excluding it from the map is what stops "I'm a project manager" appearing in the context strip and skewing the balance bar.
- **`tag`** on an option — applied to the submission as `tags[<name>]=true` alongside the static `submissionTags`. This is what carries the role to Cakemail.
- **`lens`** on an option — a standing instruction shown the moment that answer is picked *and repeated above every later question*. I went past your literal ask here: a one-off note at question 0 is forgotten by question 3, and all eight questions say "you", so the manager instruction has to persist to do its job.

The role question (`index.mdx:82`) offers Scrum Master / part-time SM / project manager / manager, tagged `role-scrum-master`, `role-part-time-sm`, `role-project-manager`, `role-manager`. Plain Team Member is gone as you asked. The manager option carries: *"Answering as a manager: think about where your Scrum Master spent their time, not where you spent yours."* I added the "not where you spent yours" half because without it the instruction is easy to read past.

Also fixed a latent bug next door: `MapMoveResults.astro` rendered a context answer with no `mapSentence` as a bare icon beside an empty line. Profile questions no longer reach it, but the guard was wrong regardless.

## Verification

Drove the actual quiz in headless Chromium, twice (as Manager, as Scrum Master):

- Profile step shows no progress bar; the eight questions run "Step 1 of 8" through "Step 8 of 8".
- The lens appears on the profile step and on all eight questions for the manager, on none of them for the Scrum Master, and doesn't leak onto the capture card.
- Intercepted the signup POST: it carries `tags[sm-role-ai]` **and** `tags[role-project-manager]`, and redirects with the profile answer in the query (`?a=role-2.q1-1…`).
- Loaded that results URL: the role doesn't leak into the result, zero empty context rows, no page errors.

Plus a unit check that `computeMapMove` and `computeQuizResult` both ignore the profile answer, and `astro check` at 0/0/0, `lint:tw` clean, production build green.

One note: the dev server that was already running returned a 500 until I restarted it. That was a stale server predating the schema change, not the change itself — the production build was green throughout.

## Two things to decide

**Tag naming.** I used bare `role-*`. They live on a shared list alongside `sm-role-ai`, `aiquiz`, `signuppopup` and so on, so if a second quiz ever asks about role these collide. `smq-role-manager` would be safer but uglier. Cheap to change now, expensive once contacts carry the tags.

**The copy pass is still ahead of us**, and this made it more urgent, not less. The eight questions and roughly thirty result sentences are in Scrum Master voice ("the highest-value thing a *Scrum Master* does", "one earliest and most important activities for a ScrumMaster"). The quiz now tells a manager it knows they're a manager and then hands them a Scrum Master's map. Say the word and I'll do the tightening pass across all eight questions and their result sentences, or start with q1, which is the one question no manager can currently answer honestly.

One question at a time. In each case we also need to ask if we can tighten the question itself repeating statements like: "Think back over the last couple of sprints." - it becomes repetitive.

Also answers like a bit of both don't scan well. Each answer should read as individually sensible.

content.text:
Starting with q1. First, the repetition inventory, since it shapes every question after this one:

- **"Think about / Think back"** opens q1, q6, q7, q8 — half the quiz.
- **"the last couple of sprints"** is in q1, q4, q5, *and* the intro, the how-it-works strip, the section blurb, `heroBody` and `description`. A taker meets it three times before question 1.
- **"When did you last…"** opens q4, q7, q8.

So the fix isn't only deleting the phrase, it's varying the openings so eight questions don't have three shapes between them. I'd anchor the timeframe **once**, in q1, and let it carry.

There's also a mechanical reason your "a bit of both" instinct is right: `randomizeOptions: 'shuffle'` is on, so options appear in a different order every time. Anything that points at its neighbours ("both", "that was most of it", "some, but…") is pointing at whatever landed above it, which changes per visit. Every option has to be readable cold, with no siblings in view.

## q1

**Question:**

> Over the last couple of sprints, where did most of your hours actually go?

One sentence instead of two. "Think back over" goes; "Over the last couple of sprints" keeps the anchor, and this is the one question that should carry it. The old second half said the same thing twice ("where the hours really went" / "what took up most of them"), so I kept one.

**Answers:**

```yaml
- text: 'Running the Scrum events and keeping everyone coordinated.'
  score: 0
  bucket: slipping
- text: 'Some keeping the team running, some working through things with people.'
  score: 1
  bucket: mixed
- text: 'Conversations, conflict, and getting people aligned.'
  score: 2
  bucket: gaining
- text: 'The events, plus my own delivery work. The role only gets part of my week.'
  score: 0
  bucket: context
```

What changed and why:

- **a** loses "That was most of it." — a tack-on that answers a question already asked, and one that reads oddly when the option lands first in a shuffle.
- **b** was the real offender: *"A fairly even split between keeping things running and the harder human work"* describes a **ratio**, not work. Every other option names something you did; this one named a proportion. Now it names both halves as activities, so it stands on its own.
- **c** loses "Mostly the human stuff" — "stuff" is doing no work and "mostly" is comparative. The three nouns are the answer.
- **d** loses the parenthetical list, which was the clunkiest line in the question. The second sentence is what actually matters and it now says it plainly.

**One open choice.** Option **a** says "the Scrum events". A project manager who picked that role at q0 runs stand-ups and planning but may not call them Scrum events. Broadening to *"Running the team's meetings and keeping everyone coordinated"* covers them, at the cost of some precision for the Scrum Masters who are most of your audience. I'd keep "Scrum events": the role question means a PM has already told us who they are, and the map sentence can carry the generosity instead.

**Knock-on.** Option a's `mapSentence` and `reclaimSentence` both repeat the old wording ("running the Scrum events and keeping the team coordinated"). If you take the answer edit, those two should track it or the result reads as a different sentence from the one they picked. I'd hold those until we've done all eight questions and then do the result copy as one pass, so the voice stays consistent across it.

Want me to apply q1 as it stands, or adjust first? Then q2.
Apply these changes and then suggest ways to tweak the map and reclaim sentence. Here after make those suggestions as part of the initial offer.

Applied. Now the result copy for q1.

## Slipping answer (a)

**Current:**

> **map:** A lot of your time went to running the Scrum events and keeping the team coordinated. That's busywork and it's the least of what makes you valuable.
> **reclaim:** Reclaim the time. Running the events and keeping everyone coordinated is the first place to lean on a tool or trim back. It's expensive because it takes time away from the real value of facilitation and coaching.

Three problems. The two sentences **overlap heavily** — both open by restating the answer, and "running the events and keeping everyone coordinated" appears in full twice, so a taker who gets this as their move reads the same clause three times counting their own answer. "That's busywork" is the only line in the quiz that judges the taker rather than the work, and it sits oddly against the intro's promise of no right answers. And the reclaim line's "It's expensive because…" is the *reason*, arriving after the instruction, which buries the part that persuades.

**Suggested:**

```yaml
mapSentence: 'A lot of your hours went to running the events and keeping everyone coordinated. It has to happen, and it is the most mechanical thing you do.'
reclaimSentence: 'Reclaim the time. Coordination is the first thing a tool can take off you, and it is expensive in a way that does not show up anywhere: every hour of it is an hour not spent facilitating or coaching.'
```

The map line now states the finding without the verdict, and "it has to happen" concedes the thing a Scrum Master would otherwise argue back at you. The reclaim line stops restating the answer, leads with the action, and lands the cost as the closing clause instead of a mid-sentence aside.

## Gaining answer (c)

**Current:**

> Most of your time went to the hard human work: conversations, conflict, getting people aligned. That's the part of the role GenAI can't replace, because it comes from building trust.

This one is close. The colon list now repeats the answer text almost verbatim, which is more noticeable with the tightened option. And "GenAI can't replace" is the quiz's only flat prediction; "comes from building trust" is the stronger half and it's trailing.

**Suggested:**

```yaml
mapSentence: 'Most of your hours went to the hard human work. That runs on trust you built over months, which is why it is the part of the job no tool is close to taking.'
```

**Current:**

> Your hours are split between the role and delivery work, so there's simply less Scrum Master time to spend. Judge it by what you did with the hours you had, not the ones you didn't.

I'd leave this one. It's the best-written sentence in q1: it names the constraint, refuses to score it as a gap, and the second sentence is the whole point of the `context` bucket. "Simply" is the only word I'd cut.

mapSentence: 'Your hours are split between the role and delivery work, so there is less Scrum Master time to spend. Judge it by what you did with the hours you had, not the ones you didn’t.'

content.text:
## q2

**Question:**

> What did the last few people who came to you actually want?

Your two sentences collapse into one without losing a word that mattered: "Picture the last few people who came to you for something" was setup for a question that then re-named the same people. Opening on "What" also breaks the pattern, since q1 now opens on a time phrase.

**Answers** — only one needs anything:

```yaml
- text: 'Help getting a blocker out of the way so they could keep moving.'
  score: 1
  bucket: mixed
```

The other three stand alone already and I'd leave them exactly as they are. This one is the odd length in the set: six words against eleven, twelve and eight. With shuffle on it reads as the throwaway option wherever it lands, purely because it's visibly shorter. The added clause is consequence, not padding.

**Result copy** — one edit, two leaves:

```yaml
# gaining
mapSentence: 'People come to you for judgment and coaching. That’s the original purpose of the role: understanding context and human motivation, which GenAI does not do.'
```

Three sentences to two, using only your words — the middle and last sentences merge on a colon. Every other map line in the quiz is two sentences, so this one currently runs long in the gaining column.

**The slipping map and reclaim lines I'd leave.** There is a repeat there ("status and logistics" in the map, "status-and-logistics desk" in the reclaim) but it's a three-word noun phrase reused inside a new coinage, not the seven-word clause we cut from q1. The coinage is the better line of the two and it earns the echo.

**The context line I'd leave untouched.** It's the best sentence in q2.

## One thing I considered and am recommending against

`People don't really come to me for anything` sits in the soft context strip and can never become the recommendation. That looks like the same case as q6's "impediments never surface" and q7's "no PO to coach", where you deliberately let a `context` answer win the move because not-your-fault isn't the same as not-important.

I don't think it is the same case. Your own line says *"It can mean the team is genuinely self-sufficient, or that you've drifted out of their orbit. If a team that brings its Scrum Master nothing is rarely self-sufficient, there's no ambiguity to preserve, and this becomes the same case as q6's impediments that never surface: a real problem, named without blame, that should be able to land in the move block instead of the soft context strip.

**Context answer, rewritten.** Modelled on your q6 context pair, which is the closest analogue — the map line observes, the redirect line instructs:

```yaml
- text: 'People don’t really come to me for anything.'
  score: 0
  bucket: context
  icon: 'people'
  mapSentence: 'People aren’t coming to you at all. There’s a reason for that, and right now you don’t know what it is.'
  redirectSentence: 'Start by finding out why people don’t come to you. Ask two or three of them directly. Until you know the reason, you’re guessing at what the team needs from you.'
```

No metaphor, no "worth sitting with", and the self-sufficient reading is gone. The map line states the finding and names the gap as a gap in *what you know*; the redirect gives the one action.

```yaml
redirectPriority: ['q2', 'q4', 'q7', 'q8', 'q5', 'q6']
```

If nobody brings you anything, that sits upstream of every coaching gap below it — you can't coach people who don't come to you, so finding out why has to happen before "put the time into coaching" is actionable advice. If you'd rather keep q4 as the top recommendation, second place works too; I'd just avoid putting it below q8.

One behaviour worth knowing: a redirect-eligible context answer sets `wellPositioned` to false. So someone who answers well everywhere *except* this one now gets the move instead of "you're well positioned", which is the right outcome under your framing and was not the case before.
